Chapter 13: The Practice of Gratitude and the Joy of Enough.
You know, in a world that’s always whispering, "get more, be more, have more," it’s surprisingly easy to forget what we already have. Gratitude often gets left behind—something we only remember when everything's going our way. But for Montaigne, gratitude was a daily habit. It was a way of looking at the world that could turn even the simplest moments into something meaningful.
Just imagine someone who's been hustling for years, suddenly stopping to notice the sunlight pouring through their window, or the sound of a friend's laughter, or even the taste of fresh bread. Those little things we usually rush past—they start to feel like treasures.
Now, don’t get me wrong—gratitude isn’t about pretending life is perfect or ignoring the tough stuff. It’s about seeing the good that sits right alongside the hard parts. It’s shifting your focus, just a little, from what’s missing to what’s already right here.
Think about this: there’s a story of someone who spent months battling illness. When their strength finally returned, every step, every deep breath—even every meal—felt like a gift. The struggle made those ordinary moments shine brighter than ever.
The joy of enough? It’s a quiet kind of happiness. It’s being able to say, “This is enough,” and truly mean it. Most of us are taught to chase after the next best thing, thinking happiness is always just out of reach. But if we’re honest, that chase never really ends. Satisfaction slips through our fingers.
Gratitude breaks this cycle. It pulls your attention back to the present—to the gifts you already have. It sparks generosity, patience, and a real sense of abundance.
Here’s something to remember: practicing gratitude is simple, but it’s not always easy. It takes intention—a moment each day to pause, notice, and say thanks. Over time, this practice can change the way you see everything.
